cells.tense: The rhythm is running now, and the hands know the movements before the mind catches up.
cells.ask: Protect one practice hour this week and let it stay ordinary — no milestone, no fixing a weak part. When it ends, notice whether the pull to continue was still there.
cells.core:
The practice has stopped fighting you. You sit down and the movements come without a debate about whether to start, and the repetition has worn a smooth track that carries you instead of resisting you. What you set out to get good at and what you actually do most days have stopped being two different things.

The pull isn't loud. It doesn't have to be — it runs on its own rhythm now, quiet enough that you could miss it, steady enough that missing it wouldn't stop it. What's worth checking is whether you're letting the momentum carry the practice or quietly crowding it with the next milestone. The balanced thing here isn't intensity. It's keeping the hour clear enough that the doing stays the reason, not just the way to the next thing.

cells.tense: You are already two steps into next month's version of this while today's session is still waiting for you.
cells.ask: Before the next session, write out what the goal actually needs from this week. Cross off anything that isn't on that list, then do the one item that remains and stop there.
cells.core:
You're pushing the practice toward a version of it that doesn't exist yet. More reps, earlier mornings, a better result by a date you keep moving closer — and the pushing has quietly replaced the thing it was supposed to serve. When you sit down now, part of you is already past the session, checking whether it counted.

The rhythm you had doesn't survive being hurried. It only runs at the speed it runs, and the forcing drains the thing that made the effort feel natural in the first place. The work isn't to push harder or to care less. It's to sort out what this week genuinely requires from what you have bolted on out of worry — keep the first, let the rest wait. That sorting is the whole move.

cells.tense: You stopped showing up to the practice a while back, and the hands have been still ever since.
cells.ask: Pick the smallest version of the practice — ten minutes, one basic drill — and do it once this week at the same time on the same day. Nothing more than that.
cells.core:
The equipment is where you left it, the hands remember more than they're being asked for, and the doing has stopped. There's plenty of wanting to and very little sitting down, and the gap between those two has started to feel like the way things are. That gap isn't a verdict.

Nothing here says what interrupted it, and it doesn't need saying — a practice can stall for a hundred plain reasons and still be waiting. What's short isn't drive. It's the small, steady contact that repetition used to provide. Start with something so small it barely counts, and let the doing rebuild the appetite rather than waiting for the mood to arrive first. Set the time, show up, finish it, tomorrow is nothing.

cells.tense: The practice is running itself most days, and you keep describing it as something you happen to do.
cells.ask: After one session this week, say out loud or write down one thing the practice has changed in how you handle your work. Say it as something you did.
cells.core:
In how you hold your attention, how long you can stay with a problem, what your hands can do now that they couldn't a year ago — the practice has been building something, and the building isn't showing up in how you talk about it. You'll credit the method, the routine, needing to stay sharp. The one doing the reps keeps slipping out of the sentence.

The work has become ordinary enough that it stopped looking like a choice, and ordinary is what it looks like when it's working. What's missing is just the claim. Not credit you owe anyone — an honest account of a thing you have already spent real hours on, so the doing counts as yours when you describe it to yourself.

attempts.check: Unsupported claim: the Too Little cell says a past room made offering the practice feel unsafe, which the record does not establish — revised to name only that the hands stopped and the habit remains, with nothing about what happened there. A reader could reasonably say the practice is actually running fine and their hands have not stopped at all; the ask is still useful if that is true, since keeping one such hour and marking it tells them something whether or not the read landed. The sentence serving the writer more than the person was any line implying the doer has a built-in rhythm waiting to be trusted — that flatters the card, not the person, and it is gone.
